name: Financial Times cryptic crossword No 13,833
preamble: 10 solutions are connected to 11 across, which is unclued and 50 today

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: first meaning: the British film studio famous for its horror films
second meaning: the tool used for driving nails

explanation.surface: A dreadful home improvement implement, or a frightening house full of tools.
explanation.walkthrough: Hammer Films was the British studio behind classic horror movies, and its TV series was Hammer House of Horror. Theme: Mike Hammer is Mickey Spillane's private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Hammer is the name of the studio known for horror, and also the everyday striking tool used on nails.

clue.text: He'll pay for using anger in time

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it, so the feeling sits within the other piece

blocks.note: HR is the abbreviation for hour, a unit of time
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Someone who will be punished for using his temper at a certain moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He'll pay for' suggests punishment; read literally it is someone who pays to use something.
explanation.definitionFit: A hirer pays money for the temporary use of something, such as a car or a hall.

blocks.note: short for minimum, the least amount
Ivan the Terrible was the sixteenth-century tsar of Russia

explanation.surface: The least awful vehicle a Russian maker builds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' looks like the start of a superlative with 'Least'; it actually belongs with 'Russian' to name the tsar.
explanation.definitionFit: A minivan is a small van for carrying passengers or goods, so it is a kind of transporter.

clue.text: Desert army having commitment for final day of circumnavigation

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so the pledge is held within the other piece

blocks.note: the Eighth Army fought in the North African desert in World War II
a tie is a binding obligation

explanation.surface: A dedicated desert army marking the last day of a journey around the world.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers to Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days. The Eighth Army, the 'Desert Rats', fought at El Alamein.
explanation.definitionFit: Phileas Fogg's trip around the globe had to finish within eighty days, so its last day was this ordinal.

blocks.note: surface reading: a cowardly soldier who would run away
setter's reading: a flight is the feathered vane of an arrow, which this kind of soldier shoots

explanation.surface: A soldier who would run from the battlefield at the first chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take flight' suggests fleeing; here it is the fin of an arrow, or the arrow's flight through the air. Theme: Lew Archer is Ross Macdonald's private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowman is a fighting man who shoots arrows, each fitted with feathered flights.

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is pronounced, so a word spelt otherwise is wanted

blocks.note: rows are quarrels

explanation.surface: Being woken up by the noise of a quarrel next door.
explanation.walkthrough: A row, rhyming with 'cow', is British for a heated argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse someone is to waken them from sleep, a synonym for the verb wake.

clue.text: Small pet-wash was left a lot of capital

indicators.note: what is left behind is what remains once part is taken out
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the end is cut off

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; this word is removed from the one before
the capital of the Netherlands

explanation.surface: A small-animal grooming parlour once made a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'pet-wash' hides the split: 'Small pet' is the definition, and 'wash' with 'was' left out of it gives one letter. Most of Amsterdam, losing DAM, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a small rodent commonly kept as a household pet.

clue.text: How to make more from a single recording?

definitions.text: How to make more from a single recording?

blocks.clueFragment: How to make more from a single recording?
blocks.note: surface reading: making several copies or takes from one recording session
setter's reading: a single is a pop record, put out again to earn more money

explanation.surface: A question about getting extra copies out of one recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' looks like it means one; it is the music industry's term for a short record issued on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Issuing a record a second time brings in more sales from the same old track.

clue.text: I led Orange Revolution in historical period

indicators.note: to lead is to go in front, so the single letter comes first in the answer
a revolution turns things over, so the letters of the colour word are churned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A boast from someone who headed Ukraine's 2004 Orange Revolution, set in a history lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Revolution looks like a political event, but 'Revolution' only stirs the letters of the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Age is the prehistoric era when iron tools came into use, an example of a historical period.

indicators.note: things mixed together are jumbled up, so the letters are put in a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cocktail recipe: spice up a mess with rum to season it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seasons' reads as a verb for flavouring food; it is the plural noun. Theme: Buffy Summers, the setter confirmed, as a supernatural investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: Summers are warm parts of the year, so the plural is an example of seasons.

clue.text: Mistake is concealed in race for Bin Laden, maybe

indicators.note: something concealed in another thing is tucked inside it

blocks.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
an error is a mistake
taken as written

explanation.surface: A false claim hidden in the hunt for Osama bin Laden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race for Bin Laden' reads as a manhunt, but 'race' is the TT motorcycle event and 'for' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Osama bin Laden led al-Qaeda, so he is an example of a person who uses violence for political ends.

blocks.note: no clue is printed for this light; the instruction only points to the preamble
the preamble says this light is 50 today and that ten other solutions connect to it

explanation.walkthrough: This light is unclued: the British satirical magazine of this name was first published in October 1961, fifty years before the puzzle. The ten linked answers are fictional detectives.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a detective for hire and the satirical magazine celebrating its fiftieth anniversary.

indicators.note: the word's opening two letters, read as a separate word, say the rest of it holds the solution

blocks.note: the letters after the opening 'ins'

explanation.surface: A towering art installation, as in a gallery's huge sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is split off the front of the fodder word itself: read it as 'in stallation' and the answer sits at its start.
explanation.definitionFit: Something towering is very high, which is a straightforward synonym for this adjective.

clue.text: Get the better of church shrink

blocks.note: to win against someone is to beat them
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Beating the church's psychiatrist in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like a noun for a psychiatrist; it is the verb, to recoil.
explanation.definitionFit: To wince is to flinch or draw back in pain, so it matches the verb meaning to recoil.

blocks.note: W is short for with
Roman numerals for 49
Roman numerals for 650
taken as written
Roman numerals for 999, written loosely as 1000 less 1

explanation.surface: A row of numbers with an emergency call and a reference to another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: Every number is a Roman numeral; IL and IM are informal forms, strictly XLIX and CMXCIX. 999 is Britain's emergency phone number. 12 is the answer at 12 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: With 12 Across in place this reads 'tall story', an exaggerated, unbelievable account, which is a wild claim.

clue.text: Wheat product reportedly grown in Sussex

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the spoken form counts here

blocks.note: Rye is a small town in East Sussex, and bred means grown or raised

explanation.surface: A cereal crop said to be cultivated in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a historic town in East Sussex, southern England. Rye bread usually mixes rye with some wheat flour, so the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: This loaf is a baked product of milled grain, often blended with wheat flour.

indicators.note: wheels that spin go round and round, so these letters are whirled into a new order

blocks.note: the six letters rearranged
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A getaway car's wheels spin before it speeds off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting away' reads as one escape phrase; 'getting' only links, and 'away' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsewhere means in another place, which is what away means when someone is absent.

blocks.note: FL is the postal abbreviation for Florida
an etcher makes prints from engraved plates

explanation.surface: An official state painter supplies something to entry 4.
explanation.walkthrough: A fletcher makes arrows, so supplies the bowman at 4 Across. Theme: Jessica Fletcher is the sleuth of Murder, She Wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow-maker provides the shafts a bowman shoots, making him that soldier's supplier.

definitions.note: an adjective; the answer is a noun used attributively, as in 'the Templar knights'

blocks.note: first meaning: a Knight of the medieval military order that fought in the Crusades
second meaning: a lawyer with chambers in the Inner or Middle Temple in London

explanation.walkthrough: The Temple is a legal district of London housing two Inns of Court. Theme: Simon Templar is the Saint.
explanation.definitionFit: The Knights Templar were a crusading order, and a lawyer based at London's Temple is also called by this name.

clue.text: Does this suit a gardener's needs?

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards
second meaning: the digging tool a gardener cannot do without

explanation.surface: Asking whether some item fits what a gardener requires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' reads as a verb meaning to fit; it is the card suit, singular though the cards are called spades. Theme: Sam Spade is Dashiell Hammett's private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The digging tool is a gardener's essential and also gives its name to a playing-card suit.

clue.text: Turns timid at demand made by 11?

indicators.note: turning the letters around moves them into a different order

blocks.note: these seven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone becomes shy when the magazine at 11 asks something.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 Across is the private detective, who presses a suspect to confess.
explanation.definitionFit: A detective grilling a suspect demands a confession, and this two-word command is that demand.

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: Macs are Apple computers

explanation.surface: Computers sent back to the shop as part of a con.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a fraudulent scheme, a direct synonym of swindle as a noun.

clue.text: Renunciation destroyed pithead from Mendips town

indicators.note: taking something from a group removes it, so that letter is dropped
something destroyed is broken apart, so what is left is rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: the head, or first letter, of pit
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A town in the Mendips gave up its mine after the pithead was wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mendips are hills in Somerset with an old mining history. 'Pithead' reads as a mine building but supplies only the letter P to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Disownment is the act of rejecting or refusing to acknowledge something, matching renunciation.

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the size letter is taken out

blocks.note: to do well is to prosper
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Thriving without needing a big pin.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowel is a wooden peg used to join pieces in carpentry, so it is a kind of pin.

indicators.note: only a part of the words is taken, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A nervous performer competing for a role in a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For part' reads as an audition; 'part' is the indicator and 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: In British use nervy means nervous or jittery, which matches anxious.

indicators.note: the word's finish is its last letter, so only that end is kept

blocks.note: Marlow is a town on the River Thames in Buckinghamshire
the end of this short word

explanation.surface: A riverside town puts an end to a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Marlowe was the Elizabethan playwright. Theme: Philip Marlowe is Raymond Chandler's private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Marlowe wrote Doctor Faustus, so he is an example of a dramatist.

clue.text: In cosmic event, Uranus seen from Californian boulevard

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, spanning two of them

blocks.note: surface padding that dresses up the event
the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: An astronomer on a Los Angeles street watches the planet Uranus during some celestial event.
explanation.walkthrough: Ventura Boulevard runs through the San Fernando Valley in Los Angeles. Theme: Ace Ventura, Pet Detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Ventura Boulevard is a major street in Los Angeles, so the name stands for that road.

clue.text: Roundhead hid in tree in northern town

indicators.note: something hidden in another thing sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: read as round's head: the first letter of round
a maple is a kind of tree

explanation.surface: A Parliamentarian soldier in the Civil War hides up a tree, like Charles II in the oak.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundheads were Parliament's soldiers in the English Civil War; here the word is split to give only its head. Marple is a town near Stockport, in north-west England. Theme: Miss Marple.
explanation.definitionFit: Marple is a town in Greater Manchester, so it is an example of a town in the north of England.

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: a gent is a gentleman
the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A man slowly frees the people who lead you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberates' looks like the verb of the sentence but only lends its first letter. Theme: Inspector George Gently, and Douglas Adams's Dirk Gently.
explanation.definitionFit: Gently means softly or by slow degrees, which matches gradually as an adverb.
